episode_title: How to Find Product-Market Fit and Measure It
content:
Lenny: Welcome to the podcast. Today I am thrilled to speak with Rahul Vohra, the founder and CEO of Superhuman. Rahul, product-market fit is the holy grail of startups, yet most people have no quantifiable way of measuring it. How did you change that at Superhuman?

Rahul Vohra: When we started Superhuman in 2015, we didn't launch for several years. The biggest fear every founder has is launching too early and realizing nobody wants what you built. I searched for a quantitative benchmark for product-market fit. I found Sean Ellis, who ran early growth at Dropbox and Eventbrite. He had discovered a leading indicator: ask your existing users, 'How would you feel if you could no longer use the product?' Options: Very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, not disappointed.

Ellis benchmarked hundreds of startups. Those that struggled to grow almost always had less than 40% answering 'very disappointed'. Those that had strong traction almost always had over 40% answering 'very disappointed'. When we first surveyed our early users at Superhuman in 2017, only 22% said they would be 'very disappointed'. That was devastating, but it gave us a measurable metric to optimize.

Lenny: So what was the exact process you built to raise that 22% above 40%?

Rahul Vohra: We built what we call the Product-Market Fit Engine. It has four systematic steps.

Step 1: Segment your audience to find your true High-Expectation Customers (HXC). We took the people who said they would be 'very disappointed' and analyzed their job titles. They were founders, executives, investors, and managers who lived in their inboxes. When we filtered the survey results to just that persona, our score jumped from 22% to 33%.

Step 2: Analyze feedback to convert on-the-fence users into superfans. We looked at users who said 'somewhat disappointed'. We asked them: 'What is the main benefit you receive from Superhuman?' and 'How can we improve Superhuman for you?'
Crucially, we ignored the users who said 'not disappointed' completely! They will pull your product roadmap in conflicting directions and dilute your core value.

Step 3: Build your roadmap by balancing two halves: 50% of your time doubling down on what your 'very disappointed' users already love (in our case: raw speed, keyboard shortcuts, clean aesthetic), and 50% of your time addressing the main blockers of the 'somewhat disappointed' users (like mobile apps, integrations, and search).

Step 4: Track the metric religiously across cohorts. We repeated this survey every quarter. In three quarters, our PMF score moved from 22% to 33%, then 46%, and eventually passed 58%. That is how you systematically engineer product-market fit instead of waiting for lightning to strike.
